screens.title: Idempotency & Distributed Locks
screens.narratorSegment: In distributed systems, network failures and timeouts are part of daily life. This lesson focuses on two practical tools you will use to make systems correct under retries and concurrent access: idempotency and distributed locks. Idempotency answers the question, "If this operation runs more than once, will the final state be the same?" Distributed locks answer the question, "How do I ensure only one worker performs a critical task at a time across many machines?" You'll learn concrete patterns such as unique request IDs or idempotency keys, conditional updates, and event-sourced idempotent handling for messaging systems. Then we shift to coordination tools: simple Redis-based locks using SET NX EX, safe release with an ownership check via a small Lua script, and stronger primitives provided by ZooKeeper or etcd. Throughout, I will show real code samples, common mistakes like duplicate charges or deadlocks, and practical mitigations such as expiry times, fencing tokens, and recording results atomically. By the end, you will know when to design an A P I as idempotent and when to reach for a distributed lock, and how to avoid common pitfalls that cause duplicated side effects or unintended concurrent execution. Consider how a single timeout on a payment request could turn into multiple charges without these safeguards.

Module 7 › Chapter 6.8 › Idempotency & Distributed Locks
Interactive 16:9 Masterclass

Idempotency & Distributed Locks

Design APIs and background jobs so retries and concurrent workers don't produce incorrect or duplicate side effects.

In this lesson

You will see practical patterns for idempotent APIs, database checks for conditional updates, and safe distributed lock implementations with Redis and coordination services.

Coming up

Examples include a payment API with an idempotency key and a Redis lock with an atomic release Lua script to avoid accidental unlocks.

Explore Key Topics
Idempotency Keys
Client-provided UUIDs to detect and replay results safely.
Conditional Updates
Database-level guards like WHERE status = 'PENDING' to enforce one-time transitions.
Distributed Locks
Mutual exclusion using Redis or ZooKeeper to coordinate workers.
Concept Map
Idempotency ↔ Retries • Locks ↔ Mutual exclusion
Problem
Retries + at-least-once delivery can cause duplicate side effects.
Goal
Guarantee correct final state and single-run critical tasks.
Patterns
Idempotency keys, conditional updates, event sourcing, Redis locks, ZooKeeper locks.
Pitfalls
Expired locks, clock skew, single point of failure, incorrect result caching.
Key Takeaway

Design for duplicates and concurrency up front: make safe APIs with idempotency and protect single-run tasks with locks chosen to match your availability and consistency needs.

screens.title: What is Idempotency?
screens.narratorSegment: Idempotency means that performing the same operation multiple times with the same input leaves the system in the same state as performing it once. This is not just an academic property — it's the practical guarantee that makes retries safe. Imagine a network timeout after a POST: the client retries, or the queue redelivers a message. If your operation is idempotent, the second execution either does nothing new or returns the same result, avoiding duplicate side effects like extra charges or double-shipped orders. A clear misconception to avoid is thinking idempotency only applies to reads; writes must often be designed to be idempotent too. For example, marking an order as SHIPPED should be a conditional update that only proceeds when the current status is PENDING. A concrete example: a POST to charge a card accompanied by a transaction ID — if the server records the transaction result keyed by that ID, subsequent requests return the stored result. The core takeaway is this: when building endpoints and message consumers, assume retries will happen and design to make repeated processing safe. Ask yourself when a duplicate message would cause harm, and then apply idempotent patterns.

keyIdea.text: Same input, repeated executions -> same final state and result once designed correctly.

content.html:
Core Concept

What is Idempotency?

A precise definition and practical consequences for retries and messaging.
Definition • Example • Misconception
Formal definition

An operation is idempotent when multiple executions with the same inputs produce the same state and response as a single execution.

Concrete example

A payment request with a transactionId where the server stores the first result and returns it for duplicates.

Common misconception

Idempotency is not only for reads; write operations must often be guarded to avoid duplicated side effects.

Key Takeaway

Design APIs and consumers assuming retries; make result replays safe by recording and checking prior results.

Visual: idempotent flow
Request A (first)
Process and store result keyed by transactionId.
Request A (retry)
Server finds stored result and returns it without recharging.
Check before mutate
For updates, use conditional statements to only perform state changes when appropriate.

screens.title: Unique Request IDs (Idempotency Keys)
screens.narratorSegment: Using a unique request ID — commonly called an idempotency key — is the most straightforward way to make A P I calls idempotent. The client generates a unique identifier for each logical operation and sends it with the request. On the server, before performing side effects, check whether that ID has already been processed. If it has, return the stored result. If not, perform the operation, store the outcome keyed by the idempotency key, and return the result. A concrete example is a /orders or /charge endpoint where the client includes a UUID header. A common mistake is storing only a transient cache without durable persistence, which can cause duplicates if the cache is evicted. Another mistake is failing to tie the stored result atomically to the side effect; you must ensure the result is recorded in a way that survives retries and restarts. This pattern is simple to reason about and maps well to synchronous A P I calls and message processing when the key is stable for the logical operation. Unique Request IDs (Idempotency Keys) means client-generated ids plus server-side result storage ensure repeated requests return the original outcome without re-executing side effects.. In practical terms, how request ids and result caching make posts safe to retry. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Process Flow

Unique Request IDs (Idempotency Keys)

Client provides a stable ID; server stores and reuses the first result.
Step-by-step
1. Client creates idempotency key
Usually a UUID sent in a header like X-Idempotency-Key.
2. Server checks store
If key exists, return stored result.
3. If new, perform operation and store result
Record success/failure and response payload for future retries.
Key Takeaway

Ensure stored results are durable and recorded atomically with side effects to avoid gap windows that create duplicates.

Example pseudocode
# Server-side pseudocode
def create_order(request_id, order_details):
  if store.has_result(request_id):
    return store.get_result(request_id)

  # mark as in-progress or PENDING in durable store
  store.record_pending(request_id)

  result = process_order_logic(order_details)

  store.store_result(request_id, result)
  return result
Common mistake

Using only an in-memory cache allows duplicates when cache evicts. Use durable storage for production-critical flows.

screens.title: Conditional Updates & SQL Guards
screens.narratorSegment: Conditional updates are a simple and powerful idempotency pattern inside the database. Rather than blindly writing a new state, perform the update only when the current state matches an expected value. For example, changing order_status from PENDING to SHIPPED should use an update guarded by WHERE status = 'PENDING'. If the update affects zero rows, the update is a no-op and you avoid duplicate transitions. A concrete example: when shipping an order, run UPDATE orders SET status = 'SHIPPED' WHERE id = 'order123' AND status = 'PENDING'; then check the affected row count. A common misconception is that application-level checks alone are sufficient; race conditions mean only atomic database-level guards reliably prevent duplicates. Another pattern is to use database unique constraints for things like idempotency keys — attempting to insert a recorded transaction with an existing key will fail and allow you to fetch the prior result. The takeaway is to prefer atomic conditional operations in the database for state transitions and to pair them with idempotency keys when external side effects must be guarded. Conditional Updates & SQL Guards means use atomic database checks and constrained writes to ensure state transitions occur only once.. In practical terms, using database constraints and conditional statements to enforce single transitions. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Comparison

Conditional Updates & SQL Guards

Prefer atomic database-level checks to prevent duplicate state transitions.
Why conditional updates?
  • They are atomic at the database and prevent race conditions.
  • Checking affected rows gives a reliable signal whether the transition occurred.
  • Pair with idempotency keys for operations involving external services.
Misconception
Application-level checks without atomic DB guards are vulnerable to concurrent updates and lost updates.
SQL example
UPDATE orders
SET status = 'SHIPPED'
WHERE id = 'order123' AND status = 'PENDING';
-- check number of affected rows to know if the update happened
Key Takeaway

Use database-level conditions and constraints as the authoritative guard against duplicate state changes.

screens.title: Monotonic Counters & Sequencing
screens.narratorSegment: Simple increment operations can be non-idempotent when a message that adds one to a counter is processed multiple times. A safer approach is to use monotonic sequences or to store the last applied sequence number so you can reject duplicates. Instead of doing increment_by(1) blindly, compute a new value based on the last known sequence or use an idempotent assignment like set_to(max(current, proposed)). For example, if you need to apply a series of offsets, attach a monotonically increasing sequence number to each operation and record the last applied sequence per key. If a replayed message has a sequence less than or equal to the stored value, skip it. A common misconception is that CAS loops alone solve everything — while CAS helps, it must be combined with durable tracking of last-applied identifiers when messages may be duplicated or reordered. The practical takeaway: for counters and sequences, record and consult a durable monotonic marker to make operations idempotent even under retries and reordering. Monotonic Counters & Sequencing means use sequence numbers or last-applied markers to make additive operations idempotent and replay-safe.. In practical terms, how to make increment operations safe and replay-friendly. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Definition

Monotonic Counters & Sequencing

Attach sequence markers to updates so replays are detected and ignored.
Pattern
  1. Assign a monotonic sequence number to each operation.
  2. Store the last-applied sequence atomically with state updates.
  3. Ignore operations with sequence <= last-applied.
Common mistake
Relying on non-durable sequence tracking or trusting message ordering across services can lead to incorrect application of updates.
Example scenario

A points system that receives messages to add points should include a message_id or sequence to ensure duplicate deliveries don't add points twice.

Key Takeaway

Use durable last-applied markers and sequences to preserve correctness when messages are duplicated or reordered.

screens.title: Event Sourcing and Natural Idempotency
screens.narratorSegment: Event sourcing treats each change as an immutable event. Because events are facts that describe a change, replaying the same event does not create a new semantic result; the final state converges to the same outcome if event handlers are idempotent or designed to tolerate replay. In practice, event consumers must still guard against duplicate side effects: if a consumer triggers an external action when processing an event, it should deduplicate by event ID or persist idempotent markers. A concrete example: emitting an OrderPlaced event is safe; if your payment service charges a card when it sees OrderPlaced, that service must ensure it only charges once per event ID by storing the processed event IDs. A common misconception is that event sourcing automatically eliminates duplicates everywhere — it helps with state reconstruction but external side effects still require deduplication. The important insight is to separate event storage from side-effect execution and to make handlers idempotent or check processed event IDs before calling external systems. Event Sourcing and Natural Idempotency means immutable events enable safe replays, but side-effecting consumers must still deduplicate by event id.. In practical terms, why immutable events make replay safe. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Architecture

Event Sourcing and Natural Idempotency

Events are immutable facts; design handlers to be idempotent when invoking side effects.
Why events help
  • Events are immutable and can be replayed to reconstruct state.
  • Handlers can be written to be idempotent by checking an event ID store.
  • External side effects still require explicit deduplication.
Example pattern

On receiving an event, first check if event_id exists in processed_events. If not, perform side effect and mark the event as processed within the same durable transaction if possible.

Key Takeaway

Event sourcing simplifies state recovery; always deduplicate before executing external effects triggered by events.

screens.title: Distributed Locks — Purpose & Models
screens.narratorSegment: Distributed locks coordinate access to a shared resource so only one process can run a critical section at a time. Use them when you must guarantee mutual exclusion for tasks like running a scheduled cleanup job on exactly one host, migrating schema safely, or updating a shared cache entry non-atomically. However, locks are not a cure-all: they introduce availability and complexity trade-offs. A common misconception is to reach for locks for every concurrency problem; often idempotency or conditional updates are simpler and more robust. When you do opt for a lock, choose an implementation that matches your consistency needs. Lightweight Redis locks are fast and simple but require careful handling of expiration and ownership. Coordination systems like ZooKeeper and etcd offer stronger ownership semantics via ephemeral nodes tied to client sessions, making automatic release on disconnect more reliable. The practical rule of thumb is: prefer idempotency and database guards for data correctness, and use locks when you genuinely need single-run behavior across machines. In practical terms, when and why to use locks across processes. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Core Concept

Distributed Locks — Purpose & Models

Coordinate work across many processes when single-run semantics are required.
When to use locks
  • Only when mutual exclusion across machines is required.
  • Schedule or coordination tasks that must run once globally.
  • Protect non-atomic cross-system operations that cannot be made idempotent.
Choosing a model
Redis-based locks are fast and simple. ZooKeeper/etcd provide session-backed ephemeral nodes that auto-release on disconnect. Choose based on the required safety and operational complexity.
Misconception
Locks solve concurrency, but they don't eliminate the need for careful expiry handling and ownership checks; they add operational overhead.

screens.title: Redis Locks with SET NX EX
screens.narratorSegment: A common lock implementation uses Redis SET with NX and EX flags: SET key value NX EX seconds. NX ensures the key is only set if absent, and EX gives the key a TTL so a crashed process doesn't hold the lock forever. The acquiring process should store a unique owner value as the lock's value so it can verify ownership before releasing the lock. Releasing should be atomic: use a small Lua script that checks the value matches the owner and deletes the key only then. A concrete example is a cleanup job where each worker attempts SET cleanup_lock worker123 NX EX 60 and proceeds if successful. A common pitfall is deleting the lock without verifying ownership — if the lock expires and another worker acquires it, an old process might delete the new owner's lock. The Lua check prevents that. Also be mindful of TTLs: if the job can exceed the expiry, consider renewing the TTL safely or use a stronger coordination service. content.html:
Implementation

Redis Locks with SET NX EX

Acquire with NX + EX and release with an ownership-checked Lua script.
Python-style example
# Acquire lock
if redis_client.set('my_resource_lock', 'locked_by_A', nx=True, ex=30):
  try:
    # perform critical work
    pass
  finally:
    # atomic release using Lua script to ensure ownership
    lua = '''
if redis.call("get",KEYS[1]) == ARGV[1] then
  return redis.call("del",KEYS[1])
else
  return 0
end
'''
    redis_client.eval(lua, 1, 'my_resource_lock', 'locked_by_A')
else:
  # failed to acquire
  pass
Pitfalls & mitigations
  • Single Redis instance is a SPOF — use clustering or sentinel for HA.
  • Locks can expire while owner still runs; consider renewing TTL or fencing tokens.
  • Always use ownership checks before deleting the lock.
Key Takeaway

Redis locks are practical but require atomic release and careful expiry handling to avoid split-brain behavior.

screens.title: ZooKeeper / etcd Locks
screens.narratorSegment: ZooKeeper and etcd provide coordination primitives designed for distributed consensus. Locks in these systems are implemented with ephemeral nodes or leases tied to client sessions. When a client creates an ephemeral node to acquire a lock, a lost connection causes the node to be removed automatically, releasing the lock. This session-backed ownership reduces the risk of orphaned locks compared with naive Redis locks. These systems also support sequential nodes for orderly lock acquisition. The trade-off is operational complexity and possible performance cost: ZooKeeper and etcd prioritize consistency and correctness over raw throughput. A common misconception is that they eliminate all operational risk — while they improve automatic release semantics, they require careful deployment, monitoring, and understanding of session timeouts and leader elections. In summary, choose ZooKeeper/etcd locks when correctness and strong ownership semantics matter more than the simplicity and speed of a Redis-based approach. Comparison

ZooKeeper / etcd Locks

Use ephemeral nodes or leases tied to sessions for stronger ownership semantics than simple key/value locks.
How session-backed locks work

Client creates an ephemeral node or obtains a lease. If the client disconnects, the node/lease is removed, freeing the lock automatically.

Pros

  • Strong consistency and ordered acquisition primitives.
Cons & operational notes

screens.title: Common Pitfalls: Expiry, Clock Skew, & Deadlock
screens.narratorSegment: When using idempotency patterns and distributed locks, several operational pitfalls can cause subtle failures. First, expiry: Redis locks use an expiration time to avoid permanent deadlocks, but if the job runs longer than the expiry the lock may expire and allow another worker to acquire it, causing concurrent execution. The mitigation is to either renew the TTL safely or use fencing tokens so the new lock holder can detect stale operations. Second, clock skew and time-based logic can cause inconsistent expiry behavior across clients; rely on server-side time or coordination rather than trusting unsynchronized clocks. Third, single point of failure: a single Redis instance used as a lock store can become a critical outage point; use clustering or sentinel for high availability or prefer consensus systems for stronger guarantees. Finally, a mistaken deletion without ownership check will remove another process's lock — always verify ownership before delete using an atomic Lua script. The takeaway is to treat locks as operational primitives that require careful design, monitoring, and fallback strategies. content.html:
Pitfalls

Expiry, Clock Skew, & Deadlock

Understand operational hazards and mitigation strategies.
Expiry too short

If a lock expires while the owner still runs, another process may acquire it and cause concurrent execution.

Clock skew

Different node clocks can make expiry and renewal logic unreliable; prefer server-based time and leases.

Ownership deletion

Deleting a lock without verifying the owner can remove another process's lock — use atomic checks to prevent this.

Mitigations
  • Renew TTL or use fencing tokens if work can exceed expiry.
  • Prefer coordination systems for stronger ownership semantics.
  • Use HA Redis or clusters to avoid SPOF.

screens.narratorSegment: Let's walk through the hands-on scenario: a /api/charge endpoint that must be idempotent. The A P I should accept userId, amount, and a transactionId supplied by the client. content.html:
Hands-on Activity

Designing an Idempotent Payment API

API design, server flow pseudocode, and common mistakes to avoid.
API Design

POST /api/charge accepts userId, amount, and transactionId (client-generated). The server uses transactionId as the idempotency key.

Common mistake

Charging before persisting a PENDING entry can create a gap where a retry re-charges. Persist a PENDING record first.

Server-side pseudocode
def charge(userId, amount, transactionId):
  status = database.get_transaction_status(transactionId)
  if status == 'SUCCESS' or status == 'FAILED':
    return database.get_transaction_result(transactionId)

  # record PENDING atomically so retries see in-progress state
  database.record_transaction(transactionId, 'PENDING', amount)

  # attempt external charge
  success = external_gateway.charge_card(userId, amount)

  if success:
    database.record_transaction(transactionId, 'SUCCESS', amount)
    return { 'status': 'SUCCESS' }
  else:
    database.record_transaction(transactionId, 'FAILED', amount)
    return { 'status': 'FAILED' }

screens.title: Key Concepts
screens.narratorSegment: Let's summarize the core ideas to carry forward. First, idempotency means repeated execution with the same input leads to the same final state; implement it with idempotency keys, conditional updates, counters with last-applied markers, or event sourcing. Second, idempotency is essential when dealing with retries, timeouts, and at-least-once messaging to avoid duplicate side effects like double charges. Third, distributed locks provide mutual exclusion across processes and are useful for single-run background jobs, but they introduce operational complexity: expiry, ownership verification, clock skew, and potential single points of failure. When choosing an approach, prefer idempotent designs for data correctness and reach for locks only when exclusivity across machines is required. Always persist idempotency markers durably, verify lock ownership before releasing, and plan for TTLs and renewals. Carry these principles into A P I and worker design so your system behaves correctly even when networks and nodes fail.

fullNarratorScript:
In distributed systems, network failures and timeouts are part of daily life. This lesson focuses on two practical tools you will use to make systems correct under retries and concurrent access: idempotency and distributed locks. Idempotency answers the question, "If this operation runs more than once, will the final state be the same?" Distributed locks answer the question, "How do I ensure only one worker performs a critical task at a time across many machines?" You'll learn concrete patterns such as unique request IDs or idempotency keys, conditional updates, and event-sourced idempotent handling for messaging systems. Then we shift to coordination tools: simple Redis-based locks using SET NX EX, safe release with an ownership check via a small Lua script, and stronger primitives provided by ZooKeeper or etcd. Throughout, I will show real code samples, common mistakes like duplicate charges or deadlocks, and practical mitigations such as expiry times, fencing tokens, and recording results atomically. By the end, you will know when to design an A P I as idempotent and when to reach for a distributed lock, and how to avoid common pitfalls that cause duplicated side effects or unintended concurrent execution. Consider how a single timeout on a payment request could turn into multiple charges without these safeguards.

By the end of these screens you will be able to define idempotency precisely and explain why it is essential when clients or queues retry requests. You'll identify common scenarios that become problematic without idempotency, such as duplicate payments, double inventory deductions, or repeated notifications. You'll also be able to describe concrete strategies for making operations idempotent: client-provided unique request IDs, conditional database updates, monotonically increasing counters, and event-sourcing approaches that naturally tolerate replay. Finally, you'll understand why distributed locks exist: to ensure a single instance of a job or access to a shared resource across multiple machines. Each objective is paired with a short mnemonic to help you remember when to use it and a verified competency milestone that signals you've implemented the pattern correctly in a design or code exercise. As you study, think about the last time you retried a web request—what would happen in your system if that same message arrived twice? This mental check helps map objectives to real engineering choices.

This second objectives screen expands the skills you need to apply and reason about safeguards. You'll learn concrete strategies: how to implement unique request IDs and cache results on the server so retries return the original response, how to perform conditional updates in the database to avoid duplicate state transitions, and how event-sourcing designs make replays safe by treating events as immutable facts. You'll also study the core challenges of distributed locks: expiration, ownership, clock skew, and single points of failure. Finally, you will practice selecting trade-offs: simple Redis locks offer speed but carry risks, while ZooKeeper and etcd provide stronger ownership semantics at the cost of extra complexity. Each objective contains a small mnemonic and a verification milestone so you can demonstrate the pattern in code or architecture diagrams. When you study, imagine building a payment endpoint and a worker that must run a data-cleanup job on only one host; these concrete scenarios connect objectives to real design choices.

Idempotency means that performing the same operation multiple times with the same input leaves the system in the same state as performing it once. This is not just an academic property — it's the practical guarantee that makes retries safe. Imagine a network timeout after a POST: the client retries, or the queue redelivers a message. If your operation is idempotent, the second execution either does nothing new or returns the same result, avoiding duplicate side effects like extra charges or double-shipped orders. A clear misconception to avoid is thinking idempotency only applies to reads; writes must often be designed to be idempotent too. For example, marking an order as SHIPPED should be a conditional update that only proceeds when the current status is PENDING. A concrete example: a POST to charge a card accompanied by a transaction ID — if the server records the transaction result keyed by that ID, subsequent requests return the stored result. The core takeaway is this: when building endpoints and message consumers, assume retries will happen and design to make repeated processing safe. Ask yourself when a duplicate message would cause harm, and then apply idempotent patterns.

Using a unique request ID — commonly called an idempotency key — is the most straightforward way to make A P I calls idempotent. The client generates a unique identifier for each logical operation and sends it with the request. On the server, before performing side effects, check whether that ID has already been processed. If it has, return the stored result. If not, perform the operation, store the outcome keyed by the idempotency key, and return the result. A concrete example is a /orders or /charge endpoint where the client includes a UUID header. A common mistake is storing only a transient cache without durable persistence, which can cause duplicates if the cache is evicted. Another mistake is failing to tie the stored result atomically to the side effect; you must ensure the result is recorded in a way that survives retries and restarts. This pattern is simple to reason about and maps well to synchronous A P I calls and message processing when the key is stable for the logical operation. Unique Request IDs (Idempotency Keys) means client-generated ids plus server-side result storage ensure repeated requests return the original outcome without re-executing side effects.. In practical terms, how request ids and result caching make posts safe to retry. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Conditional updates are a simple and powerful idempotency pattern inside the database. Rather than blindly writing a new state, perform the update only when the current state matches an expected value. For example, changing order_status from PENDING to SHIPPED should use an update guarded by WHERE status = 'PENDING'. Distributed locks coordinate access to a shared resource so only one process can run a critical section at a time. Use them when you must guarantee mutual exclusion for tasks like running a scheduled cleanup job on exactly one host, migrating schema safely, or updating a shared cache entry non-atomically. However, locks are not a cure-all: they introduce availability and complexity trade-offs. A common misconception is to reach for locks for every concurrency problem; often idempotency or conditional updates are simpler and more robust. When you do opt for a lock, choose an implementation that matches your consistency needs. Lightweight Redis locks are fast and simple but require careful handling of expiration and ownership. Coordination systems like ZooKeeper and etcd offer stronger ownership semantics via ephemeral nodes tied to client sessions, making automatic release on disconnect more reliable. The practical rule of thumb is: prefer idempotency and database guards for data correctness, and use locks when you genuinely need single-run behavior across machines. A common lock implementation uses Redis SET with NX and EX flags: SET key value NX EX seconds. NX ensures the key is only set if absent, and EX gives the key a TTL so a crashed process doesn't hold the lock forever. Releasing should be atomic: use a small Lua script that checks the value matches the owner and deletes the key only then. ZooKeeper and etcd provide coordination primitives designed for distributed consensus. Locks in these systems are implemented with ephemeral nodes or leases tied to client sessions. When a client creates an ephemeral node to acquire a lock, a lost connection causes the node to be removed automatically, releasing the lock. This session-backed ownership reduces the risk of orphaned locks compared with naive Redis locks. These systems also support sequential nodes for orderly lock acquisition. The trade-off is operational complexity and possible performance cost: ZooKeeper and etcd prioritize consistency and correctness over raw throughput. A common misconception is that they eliminate all operational risk — while they improve automatic release semantics, they require careful deployment, monitoring, and understanding of session timeouts and leader elections. When using idempotency patterns and distributed locks, several operational pitfalls can cause subtle failures. First, expiry: Redis locks use an expiration time to avoid permanent deadlocks, but if the job runs longer than the expiry the lock may expire and allow another worker to acquire it, causing concurrent execution. The mitigation is to either renew the TTL safely or use fencing tokens so the new lock holder can detect stale operations. Second, clock skew and time-based logic can cause inconsistent expiry behavior across clients; rely on server-side time or coordination rather than trusting unsynchronized clocks. Third, single point of failure: a single Redis instance used as a lock store can become a critical outage point; use clustering or sentinel for high availability or prefer consensus systems for stronger guarantees. Finally, a mistaken deletion without ownership check will remove another process's lock — always verify ownership before delete using an atomic Lua script. Let's summarize the core ideas to carry forward. First, idempotency means repeated execution with the same input leads to the same final state; implement it with idempotency keys, conditional updates, counters with last-applied markers, or event sourcing. Second, idempotency is essential when dealing with retries, timeouts, and at-least-once messaging to avoid duplicate side effects like double charges. Third, distributed locks provide mutual exclusion across processes and are useful for single-run background jobs, but they introduce operational complexity: expiry, ownership verification, clock skew, and potential single points of failure. When choosing an approach, prefer idempotent designs for data correctness and reach for locks only when exclusivity across machines is required. Always persist idempotency markers durably, verify lock ownership before releasing, and plan for TTLs and renewals. Carry these principles into A P I and worker design so your system behaves correctly even when networks and nodes fail.

Keep these three practical reminders close when you design systems. First, always assume retries: include a unique operation ID or message ID and persist the first result. Second, prefer atomic database guards for state changes — conditional updates and unique constraints are simple and reliable. Third, if you must coordinate work across machines, use distributed locks but do so with ownership checks, expiry strategies, and an awareness of trade-offs between Redis and coordination services. A final reflection: before adding locks, ask whether idempotency or a database constraint could solve the problem more simply. This checklist will help you design robust systems that fail gracefully without creating duplicate side effects or unintended concurrent runs.
